quests.instruction: Read it slowly first, then at natural speed ([rl] and [rld] clusters).
quests.hint: 'girl' ends in [rl] and 'world' in [rld]. Keep the r-colour, then touch the tongue tip for [l].
quests.explanation: The tongue must move from the pulled-back [r] position to the ridge for [l] without adding a vowel. In 'world', finish with a voiced [d].
quests.textToSpeak: That girl has travelled all over the world.
quests.phoneticHint: 'girl' is [gɜːrl] and 'world' is [wɜːrld]: one syllable each.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a sleepy remark.
quests.hint: 'barely', 'early' and 'nearly' all have [rl].
quests.explanation: In 'early', the stressed [ɜːr] slides into [l] with no vowel between. In 'barely' and 'nearly', [r] follows a stressed vowel and [l] begins the unstressed syllable.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm barely awake; it's early, and I nearly overslept.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a news headline.
quests.hint: 'world' and 'girl' repeat the [rl] pattern; 'record' has stress on the first syllable as a noun, and 'fourteen' has final stress.
quests.explanation: Notice that 'world' flows into 'record' with no pause. 'broken by a girl' links as 'bro-ken-by-a-girl'.
quests.textToSpeak: The world record was broken by a girl of fourteen.
quests.phoneticHint: [ðə ˈwɜːrld ˈrekərd wəz ˈbroʊkən baɪ ə ˈgɜːrl əv ˌfɔːrˈtiːn].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a shopper.
quests.hint: 'clothes' ends in [ðz] in careful speech, or just [z] in fast speech; never 'cloth-es'.
quests.explanation: For the full form, put the tongue at the teeth for [ð], then go straight to [z] without a vowel. In casual speech, [ð] is dropped and it sounds like 'close'.
quests.textToSpeak: I need new clothes for the wedding.
quests.phoneticHint: 'clothes' is [kloʊðz] or [kloʊz]; 'cloth' [klɒθ] is a different word.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a hiking tip.
quests.hint: 'paths' ends with a tongue-at-teeth sound plus [s] or [z]: [pæðz] in American English, [pɑːθs] in some British accents.
quests.explanation: Either version is a two-consonant ending: put the tongue tip at the teeth, then release straight into a hiss or buzz. Never insert a vowel.
quests.textToSpeak: The paths through the forest are muddy, so bring boots.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a news comment Watch the [θ] and [ðz]/[θs] endings.
quests.hint: 'both' ends in [θ] and 'truths' ends in [ðz] or [θs]: two different endings with the tongue at the teeth.
quests.explanation: Keep the tongue tip at the teeth for the last sound in each word, and don't add a vowel. In 'truths', the [r] comes quickly after [t].
quests.textToSpeak: Both sides told half-truths, and the full story only came out later.

quests.instruction: Read it slowly first, then at natural speed (silent letters: Wednesday, February).
quests.hint: 'Wednesday' has a silent d, and 'February' is said with the first r kept: WENZ-day, FEB-roo-air-y.
quests.explanation: Say 'Wednesday' in two syllables: [ˈwenzdeɪ]. Say 'February' as [ˈfebruːeri] or [ˈfebjuːeri]; take a moment on the first r.
quests.textToSpeak: Our anniversary is on the last Wednesday in February.
commonMistakes: Saying the [d] in the first syllable of 'Wednesday'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a trusting comment.
quests.hint: 'doubt' has a silent b, 'answer' a silent w, and 'listens' a silent t.
quests.explanation: Silent letters belong to the spelling, not the sound. Say [daʊt], [ˈænsər] and [ˈlɪsənz].
quests.textToSpeak: I have no doubt she'll answer; she always listens to what people say.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a tour comment.
quests.hint: 'castle' has a silent t, 'island' a silent s, and 'knowledge' a silent k.
quests.explanation: The letters are silent, but the words keep their vowels and endings clear: 'castle' [ˈkæsəl], 'island' [ˈaɪlənd], 'knowledge' [ˈnɒlɪdʒ].
quests.textToSpeak: There's an old castle on the island, and the guide's knowledge of its history was excellent.

quests.instruction: Read it slowly first, then at natural speed (unpredictable spellings: choir, colonel).
quests.hint: 'choir' sounds like 'quire' [kwaɪər], and 'colonel' sounds like 'kernel' [ˈkɜːrnəl].
quests.explanation: Both words are spelled unpredictably: 'choir' has [kw] and a diphthong, while 'colonel' has [ɜːr] and no [l] in the middle.
quests.textToSpeak: My uncle sings in the choir, and he's also a retired colonel.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a question at a station.
quests.hint: 'guide' has a silent u, and 'queue' has the letters ue but sounds like the letter Q.
quests.explanation: 'queue' is just the letter name [kjuː]. 'guide' is [gaɪd]; the u only shows that the g is hard.
quests.textToSpeak: Could you guide me to the queue? I want to buy a ticket.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a comment about a boat.
quests.hint: 'yacht' sounds like 'yot' [jɒt], and 'height' ends with [t], not [θ].
quests.explanation: 'yacht' has a silent ch. 'height' looks like 'width' or 'length', but it ends with [t]: [haɪt].
quests.textToSpeak: The yacht was so beautiful that I forgot to check its height.
commonMistakes: Saying 'beautiful' with the stress on the second syllable

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a comment about a storm.
quests.hint: 'wind' as a noun is [wɪnd] (moving air); as a verb it is [waɪnd] (to turn).
quests.explanation: The spelling is the same, but the vowel and meaning change. The noun uses a short [ɪ]; the verb uses the diphthong [aɪ].
quests.textToSpeak: The wind was so strong that I had to wind up the car window.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a small story.
quests.hint: The first 'tear' (a rip) is [ter]; the second (from an eye) is [tɪr].
quests.explanation: Same spelling, two sounds: the rip rhymes with 'air', and the drop rhymes with 'ear'.
quests.textToSpeak: There was a tear in my sleeve, and I almost shed a tear.
commonMistakes: Using the same vowel in both words

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a story about a disagreement.
quests.hint: The argument 'row' rhymes with 'cow' [raʊ]; the paddling 'row' rhymes with 'go' [roʊ].
quests.explanation: One spelling, two vowels: [aʊ] for the noun meaning an argument, [oʊ] for the verb about boats.
quests.textToSpeak: We had a row about the boat; I wanted to row across the lake.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a café order.
quests.hint: 'espresso' is es-PRES-so (never 'expresso'), 'croissant' is close to kwah-SOHN in a French style, and 'sushi' is SOO-shee.
quests.explanation: Borrowed words keep some of their original sounds. 'espresso' stresses the second syllable; 'sushi' has a clean [ʃ] and a final [i].
quests.textToSpeak: We ordered an espresso, a croissant and some sushi.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a hotel restaurant announcement.
quests.hint: 'buffet' is buh-FAY, and 'paella' is pie-EL-ya.
quests.explanation: 'buffet' ends with a silent t: [bəˈfeɪ]. 'paella' begins with [paɪ] and has [ˈeljə] in the middle.
quests.textToSpeak: The buffet has pasta, paella and a choice of desserts.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a social update.
quests.hint: 'ballet' is ba-LAY, 'debut' is day-BYOO, and 'fiancé' is fee-ahn-SAY.
quests.explanation: These words come from French and end with a stressed syllable; the final consonant in 'ballet' and 'debut' is silent.
quests.textToSpeak: At the ballet, the young dancer made her debut, and her fiancé filmed it.
commonMistakes: Pronouncing the final t in 'ballet' and 'debut'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a travel plan.
quests.hint: 'Beijing' is bay-JING with a [dʒ] or [ʒ]; 'Doha' is DOH-ha.
quests.explanation: The second syllable of 'Beijing' carries the stress. 'Doha' has stress on the first syllable and a light [h] in the middle.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm flying to Beijing via Doha.
commonMistakes: Saying the last syllable with a hard [g], as 'Bay-ging'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a travel wish.
quests.hint: 'Peru' is puh-ROO, and 'Machu Picchu' is MAH-choo PEEK-choo.
quests.explanation: 'Peru' has stress on the second syllable. In 'Picchu', the 'cch' sounds like [tʃ], as in 'chip'.
quests.textToSpeak: One day, I'd like to visit Peru and see Machu Picchu.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a news comment Watch the place names: Chile, Qatar, Thailand.
quests.hint: 'Chile' is CHIL-ee, 'Qatar' is KUH-tar or CAT-ar, and 'Thailand' is TY-land.
quests.explanation: None of these follow English spelling rules: 'Chile' isn't 'chilly' with [ɪ], 'Qatar' starts with [k], and 'Thailand' starts with [t], not [θ].
quests.textToSpeak: Chile, Qatar and Thailand have all hosted big events.

quests.instruction: Read it slowly first, then at natural speed (stress shift: compete, competition, competitive).
quests.hint: The stress shifts: com-PETE, com-pe-TI-tion, com-PET-i-tive.
quests.explanation: -tion pulls the stress to the syllable before it, and -ive keeps the stress on 'pet'. The verb 'compete' has the stress on 'pete'.
quests.textToSpeak: They compete every year; the competition is fierce, and everyone is very competitive.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a factual comment.
quests.hint: 'origin' is OR-i-gin, and 'original' is o-RI-gi-nal.
quests.explanation: Adding -al moves the stress from the first syllable to the second. The first vowel changes from a full [ɔː] to a weak [ə].
quests.textToSpeak: The origin of the idea is unclear, but the original plan was clearly different.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a business comment Watch the stress shift: industry, industrial.
quests.hint: 'industry' is IN-dus-try; 'industrial' is in-DUS-tri-al.
quests.explanation: The stress moves one syllable to the right when -ial is added: IN-dus-try becomes in-DUS-trial. The first vowel becomes weak.
quests.textToSpeak: The industry is growing fast, and industrial jobs are in demand.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a frustrated caller.
quests.hint: 'sixth' ends in [ksθ] and 'eighth' in [tθ].
quests.explanation: In 'sixth', the hiss is followed by the tongue at the teeth for [θ]; keep the [k] and [s] tight. In 'eighth', the [t] merges with [θ]: touch the tongue at the teeth once.
quests.textToSpeak: This is the sixth time I've called, and it's the eighth day without an answer.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a measurement.
quests.hint: 'width' ends in [dθ] or [tθ], 'length' in [ŋθ] or [ŋkθ], and 'depth' in [pθ].
quests.explanation: Each ends with a stop or nasal followed by the tongue at the teeth. Keep the closure short, then release into [θ]; don't add a vowel.
quests.textToSpeak: The width, length and depth of the room are all on the plan.

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a news statistic.
quests.hint: 'fifths' ends in [fθs], 'thirds' ends in [rdz], and 'thirty' starts with [θɜːr].
quests.explanation: 'fifths' is the hardest: lip-teeth [f], then tongue-teeth [θ], then [s]. Say it slowly first. In 'thirds', the [d] and [z] blend.
quests.textToSpeak: Three-fifths of voters said yes, and two-thirds of them were under thirty.
commonMistakes: Saying 'thirty' with [t] at the start, as 'tirty'

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud at a natural pace.
quests.hint: Watch 'honest' (silent h), 'rather' [ð], 'hours' (silent h), and 'queuing' [kjuːɪŋ].
quests.explanation: This sentence combines silent letters, [ð], and the [kj] sequence. Keep the pace natural; only 'pay', 'extra', 'eight' and 'queuing' need strong beats.
quests.textToSpeak: To be honest, I'd rather pay extra than spend eight hours queuing at the airport.
quests.phoneticHint: [tə bi ˈɒnɪst aɪd ˈræðər ˈpeɪ ˈekstrə ðən ˈspend ˈeɪt ˈaʊərz ˈkjuːɪŋ ət ði ˈeərpɔːrt].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as an event announcement Watch the mixed difficulties: [rld], February, [str].
quests.hint: Check the [rld] in 'world', the tricky 'February', and the [str] in 'strong'.
quests.explanation: Say 'world' as one syllable, pronounce the first r in 'February', and start 'strong' with a quick [str] cluster.
quests.textToSpeak: Our world tour starts in February, and ticket sales have been strong so far.
quests.phoneticHint: [aʊər ˈwɜːrld ˈtʊr stɑːrts ɪn ˈfebruːeri ənd ˈtɪkɪt ˈseɪlz həv bɪn ˈstrɒŋ soʊ ˈfɑːr].

quests.instruction: Read the sentence aloud as a quality-check remark.
quests.hint: 'doubt' and 'receipt' have silent letters, 'wrong' has a silent w, and 'sixth' and 'width' end with [θ] clusters.
quests.explanation: This sentence mixes four difficulties. Say the silent-letter words as they sound, and take a little more time on 'sixth' and 'width'.
quests.textToSpeak: There's no doubt that the sixth item is the one with the wrong width; check the receipt.
quests.phoneticHint: [ðərz ˈnoʊ ˈdaʊt ðət ðə ˈsɪksθ ˈaɪtəm ɪz ðə ˈwʌn wɪð ðə ˈrɒŋ ˈwɪdθ ˈtʃek ðə rɪˈsiːt].
commonMistakes: Pronouncing the b in 'doubt' or the w in 'wrong'
